title: Precision, recall, and decision thresholds
summary: See the trade-off between catching positives and creating false alerts.
objectives: Select a threshold for a use case

sections.title: Count the different mistakes
paragraphs: A true positive is a correctly flagged positive. A false positive is an ordinary case incorrectly flagged. A false negative is a positive the system missed. Precision is true positives divided by all predicted positives; recall is true positives divided by all actual positives.

Accuracy can conceal failure when one class dominates. A system that always predicts “ordinary” on a dataset with 99% ordinary cases has 99% accuracy but zero recall for the cases that may matter most.

sections.title: A score is not a decision
paragraphs: A classifier often produces a score before making a binary decision. Raising the threshold usually reduces the number of positive predictions; lowering it usually increases them. The resulting precision and recall depend on the observed score distribution.

Choose the threshold on validation data using error costs, review capacity, and minimum requirements. When a denominator is zero, represent the metric as unavailable or follow an explicit convention. Do not silently turn an undefined result into a perfect score.

code.source:
actual = [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0]
scores = [0.95, 0.8, 0.65, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1]
for threshold in [0.3, 0.5, 0.9]:
    predicted = [int(score >= threshold) for score in scores]
    tp = sum(a == 1 and p == 1 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
    fp = sum(a == 0 and p == 1 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
    fn = sum(a == 1 and p == 0 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
    precision = tp/(tp+fp) if tp+fp else None
    recall = tp/(tp+fn) if tp+fn else None
    print(threshold, {"precision": precision, "recall": recall})
code.explanation: Use the interactive threshold lab to move the decision boundary on this same invented dataset. None of these scores is a live model benchmark.

steps: Assume reviewers can inspect at most three flagged examples.
Calculate how many cases each threshold flags.
Choose a feasible threshold and report what it misses.
practice.solution: At 0.5, three cases are flagged and two are correct; one actual positive is missed. At 0.9, only one case is flagged and two positives are missed. At 0.3, five flags exceed capacity. The choice depends on the stated constraints.
practice.expected: At threshold 0.5, precision and recall are both 2/3.

quiz.question: If no examples are predicted positive, precision is…
options: Undefined unless a convention is explicitly chosen
quiz.explanation: The precision denominator is zero. Displaying this as an unavailable value avoids a misleading claim.
